## What you build today

Let's drive our motor! We aim to get a flashed G431 ESC talking to your laptop over micro-USB (serial), with the angular sensor wired on SPI and the motor spinning under commander control.

## Electronic Speed Controller
The **B-G431B-ESC1** is ST's reference three-phase motor driver: a complete ESC on one small board, sold as an evaluation kit. Three parts of it matter for this build:

- **An STM32G431 microcontroller.** A 170 MHz Cortex-M4 with hardware floating point. Motor control recomputes the field orientation every control loop. This MCU is the reason we can.
- **A three-phase inverter with current sensing.** Six power MOSFETs drive the three motor phases, and shunt resistors on the low side report the current actually flowing in each. That measurement is what turns "spin the motor" into **torque control**. You cannot regulate a current you cannot see.

![The power stage of the B-G431B-ESC1. The six MOSFETs are the large flat packages, arranged as three half-bridges --- one per motor phase, each with a high-side and a low-side switch. The three copper tabs on the left are the U, V and W outputs you solder the motor to below, and the grey block behind is the heatsink.](/Fig/g431-power-stage.jpg){#fig-g431-power width="75%"}

- **A detachable ST-Link programmer (the daughterboard).** The small daughter board is how we program the MCU over USB, and it also carries a serial port back to your laptop. When snapped-off, the MCU cannot be reprogramed without physically resoldering it.

It also brings out a hall/encoder connector (**J8**), a CAN transceiver and a potentiometer input, none of which we use as intended. In this build J8 gets repurposed for serial, and the encoder arrives on SPI instead. Both of those reworks are below. The board is rated well above what the wing motor draws, so current is not the constraint here.

## Angular sensor

### Why the motor needs an encoder

Field-Oriented Control works by holding the stator's magnetic field roughly 90° ahead of the rotor's magnets, which is the orientation that produces the most torque per amp. To place the field there, the controller has to know where the rotor is **right now**.

Ordinary drone ESCs infer this from back-EMF, i.e the voltage the spinning rotor induces in the phase that is not currently being driven (@eq-bemf in [Module 2](02-motor.qmd)). That voltage is proportional to speed, so as the motor slows the signal sinks into the noise and the estimate falls apart. This causes *loss of synchronisation at low speed* described in [Design notes](/reference/design-notes.qmd). The AS5047P removes the guess. It measures the field of the magnet bonded to the shaft end and reports the **absolute** angle --- valid at standstill just as much as at 15 000 rpm, and correct immediately at power-on with no homing move.

### What SPI is, and why we run it at 10 MHz

The AS5047P reports angle over SPI, a four-wire synchronous bus: the controller drives the clock (**SCLK**), data goes out on **MOSI** and comes back on **MISO**, and **CS** selects the chip. Transfer speed is limited only by how fast the two ends can shift bits. We use SPI because it offers **10 MHz** communication. The reason speed matters is that the angle has to be re-read every single control loop, and a stale angle is gad: the controller ends up placing the stator field where the rotor **was**, not where it is. That error shows up as wasted current and audible noise. The same 10 MHz clock is why the wiring has to stay short, see below.


### Wiring it to the board

There is no SPI link exposed directly on the ESC board. The solution is to use the **SPI3 bus**, exposed through a few hardware modifications and matching software changes. @fig-wiring shows the four signals in context, including the MOSI tap on R14. 

::: {.callout-warning}
#### You lose the micro-USB serial link
Serial2, used by the daughterboard for serial communication will not work anymore as we are using those pins for SPI3 for the encoder instead. Flashing the ESC still works (programming runs over SWD, on different pins) but every
command and every value you read back now has to pass through a different serial.
:::


|               | SCLK | MISO | MOSI  | CS   |
|---------------|------|------|-------|------|
| **MCU GPIO**  | PB3  | PB4  | PB5   | PA15 |
| **G431B pin** | J3   | J3   | R14\* | J3   |

: SPI3 connections on the G431. \* Solder onto the outward side of the resistor. {#tbl-spi3}

![GPIOs of the G431B-ESC1 board](/Fig/b431g.jpg){#fig-g431-gpio}

::: {.callout-warning}
## Keep the SPI cables under 8 cm

Cables between encoder and ESC need to be **less than 8 cm**. At 10 MHz longer
runs start corrupting angle readings, and the symptom is a motor that behaves
erratically rather than a sensor that obviously fails.
:::

Next, use M2 screws to mount the encoder on the 3D printed bracket that sits around the motor. Check that the distance between sensor and magnet is 0.5 mm, and centered.

## Solder the motor wires
Since the pads are large, make sure to use enough heat / large tip on the soldering iron. The order of the cables UVW do not matter. 

## How to program the ESC
With the encoder and motor connected to the ESC, we can start programing the ESC!
Remap the pins in software for SPI use: in `platformio.ini` via `build_flags`, and by overwriting the `WEAK PinMap`s in `pinmap_custom.h`. See commit `18520ac` on GitHub for details.

## Firmware

Code for the B-G431B-ESC1 motor controller, using the SimpleFOC library, is in the lab repository: [FAAV-G431-ESC](https://github.com/MIT-AURA-Lab/FAAV-G431-ESC). See [Software](/reference/software.qmd) for all repositories.

## Commanding and monitoring
This is a high-level summary of [the SimpleFOC communication docs](https://docs.simplefoc.com/communication). Communication with the ESC is over **serial**, via a separate microcontroller board.

Once serial communication is established, you interact with the ESC through the **commander**, a practical interface for setting and getting values ([instructions](https://docs.simplefoc.com/commander_motor)). Ask the commander for available commands with `?`. Commands available:

| Command | Effect |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `M` | Full motor configuration |
| `F` | Get the main loop frequency |
| `L` | Turn the onboard LED on and off (useful as a comms check) |
| `T` | Set the target value --- rad, rad/s or N/m depending on control mode |
| `W` | Watchdog on/off. If no new target arrives for 1 s, target is set to zero. **On by default** |
| `R` | `R0`/`R1` disable/enable a linear ramp when changing setpoint. `RD1000` sets ramp duration to 1000 ms (default 1000 ms). Off by default |

::: callout-warning
## Careful when changing control mode

`T` means something different in each mode, position, velocity, or torque. Sending a velocity setpoint while in torque mode will do something you did not intend, with the wings attached. BE VERY CAREFUL ABOUT THIS.
:::

::: callout-note
## Checkpoint

Commander responds to `?` over serial at 115200 baud, `L` toggles the onboard LED, the sensor returns a plausible angle through a full manual rotation, and the motor spins under a `T` command.
:::


::: {.callout-important}
## To be prepared by the instructor before the session

Prepare a power source 15V 5A over USB-C.
